title: Needs and wants
job: Say what you want and don't want
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Je ne veux pas + de + N

rules.text: vouloir is the module's verb: je veux · vous voulez. Wanting to DO something is je veux plus a BARE infinitive — Je veux manger — with no word for "to" anywhere in it.
English's "want to eat" pushes a preposition into a place French keeps empty. Je veux à manger and Je veux de manger are both wrong: nothing at all stands between the two verbs.
Negation is TWO words wrapping the verb, not one word in front of it: ne before it and pas after it — Je ne veux pas. Both halves are written, however often speech drops the ne.
The negation changes the article behind it: du, de la, des, un and une all collapse to a bare de after ne … pas. Je veux du café becomes Je ne veux pas de café, never Je ne veux pas du café.

For an unmeasured amount French writes a partitive where English writes nothing at all: du pain, de la soupe, des pommes — "bread", "soup", "apples". du is de + le and des is de + les, so these are contractions before they are anything else.
Three ways of saying how much, and French picks one out loud where English can stay silent: un / une counts one whole thing, du and de la take some of a mass, des takes some of a plural.
The plural -s is WRITTEN and SILENT. une pomme and des pommes differ in speech by the little word in front and by nothing on the noun, so a learner who is only listening has to listen to the article.
A question is still the statement with a rising voice, exactly as L1-M2 taught it: Vous voulez du lait ?

words.note: vouloir, to want. je veux · vous voulez — the ending names the person, as être's did. It takes a thing (je veux un café) or a bare verb (je veux manger), and never a preposition in between.
a, in front of a masculine noun — and also the number one. French does not separate the two: un café is "a coffee" and "one coffee" at once, and the sentence decides which. Its feminine twin is une.

sentences.trap: English can leave the article out when it orders — "I want coffee". French cannot: something always stands in front of the noun, and the choice between un and du is the module's work.
sentences.sound: veux is one syllable, vuh, with the final -x silent — the eu is made with the lips rounded and the tongue forward. un is nasal: the air goes through the nose and the n is never sounded.

variations.changed: swap the thing — je veux un … is the frame
voulez for the person you are speaking to, and a rising voice makes it a question

variations.display: Je ne veux pas de café
variations.changed: the two-part negation wraps the verb — and un collapses to a bare de behind it

mistake.why: The noun cannot stand bare here: it is un café for one cup, or du café for some coffee, but never nothing at all.

sentences.usage: Ordering, asking, saying what you are after.
sentences.mnemonic: un is both "a" and "one" — French never needed two words for it.

words.note: du is de welded onto le, with two jobs. Before an uncountable noun it is the partitive — du pain, "some bread", where English writes nothing. Before a place or owner it is "of the": à côté du lit.
bread — masculine, so le pain and du pain.

sentences.trap: English has a word for this and refuses to use it: "I want some bread" and "I want bread" are both fine. French has no such choice — the partitive is not optional, and Je veux pain is not a sentence.
sentences.sound: du is one tight syllable, dü — the u is the French u, lips rounded for oo while the tongue says ee. pain is nasal, pan, and neither the i nor the n is sounded on its own.

variations.changed: swap the mass noun — du is the frame for anything uncountable and masculine
voulez and a rising voice — the partitive is unchanged

variations.display: Je ne veux pas de pain
variations.changed: du collapses to a bare de behind the negation

mistake.why: An uncountable noun still needs its partitive: du pain. Leaving it out is English showing through.

sentences.usage: Asking for a share of something rather than a whole one.
sentences.mnemonic: du = de + le: literally "of the" bread — some of it, not all of it.

words.note: The feminine partitive. de and la stay two separate words here — only le welds onto de to make du — so it is de la soupe beside du pain, and the noun's gender is what chooses between them.
soup — feminine, so la soupe and de la soupe.

sentences.trap: The gender you learned with the noun in L1-M1 comes back to charge you here: it decides du against de la, and there is nothing in the sentence itself to remind you which the noun was.
sentences.sound: de la is two light syllables, duh la. soupe is soop, with the final -e silent and no oo-oo glide on the vowel.

variations.changed: swap the feminine mass noun — de la is the frame
voulez and a rising voice, with the partitive untouched

variations.display: Je ne veux pas de soupe
variations.changed: de la collapses to a bare de behind the negation, exactly as du does

mistake.why: soupe is feminine, so its partitive is de la, not du. The gender chooses the article here as it did in L1-M1.

sentences.usage: Asking for some of something feminine — soup, water, patience.
sentences.mnemonic: Only le is greedy enough to weld onto de. la keeps its distance.

words.note: des is de welded onto les, and the plural of both un/une and du/de la: des pommes is "some apples" where English writes just "apples". Its "of the" reading stays out of L1.
apple — feminine, so une pomme and des pommes. The plural -s is written and silent: the article is the only thing the ear can hear change.

sentences.trap: English drops the word entirely in the plural — "I want apples". French will not: des is as obligatory as du, and Je veux pommes is not a sentence.
sentences.sound: des is day, with the -s silent unless a vowel follows. pommes is pom — one syllable, the final -es adding nothing at all.

variations.changed: one whole thing takes une; the plural of that is des
voulez and a rising voice, with des untouched

variations.display: Je ne veux pas de pommes
variations.changed: des collapses to a bare de behind the negation, like every other article here

mistake.why: A plural still needs des in French: des pommes. The bare noun is the English shape.

sentences.usage: Asking for a few of something countable.
sentences.mnemonic: un one, du some of a mass, des some of a heap.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "I want eat" — there is no word for "to"

words.note: to eat — the dictionary form, and the one that follows another verb with nothing in between. The -er ending is what marks it as the bare form, and it sounds exactly like é: mahn-ZHAY.

sentences.trap: English's "to" has nothing to translate into here. Je veux à manger and Je veux de manger both reach for a word the frame does not have, and both are wrong.
sentences.sound: mahn-ZHAY. The an is nasal, the g is the soft sound in the middle of "measure", and the -er ending is a clean ay.

variations.changed: swap the second verb — the gap between them stays empty
voulez and a rising voice; the infinitive does not move
ne … pas wraps the FIRST verb — the infinitive stays outside it

mistake.why: Nothing stands between vouloir and the verb it governs: Je veux manger. The à is English's "to" arriving where French has no room for it.

sentences.usage: Saying what you want to do, rather than what you want.
sentences.mnemonic: Two verbs, no bridge: veux manger.

sentences.cue: I want to drink some tea

words.note: to drink — the bare form again, following veux with nothing between them. Its -re ending marks a different verb family from manger's -er, which will matter in L1-M4.
tea — masculine, so le thé and du thé. The h does nothing at all: th is simply a t.

sentences.trap: The partitive survives the second verb: it is the tea that is uncountable, not the drinking, so du sits in front of thé exactly as it would in a shorter sentence.
sentences.sound: boire is one syllable, bwar, with the r made at the back of the throat. thé is tay — the h is silent, and the é is the sound the accent marks.

variations.cue: I want to drink some coffee
variations.changed: swap the mass noun — the frame and the partitive are untouched

variations.cue: Do you want to drink some tea?
variations.changed: voulez and a rising voice across the whole two-verb frame

variations.display: Je ne veux pas boire de thé
variations.cue: I don't want to drink any tea
variations.changed: the negation wraps veux, and du still collapses to de behind it

mistake.why: The partitive belongs to the noun, not to the sentence's shape: du thé, however many verbs stand in front of it.

sentences.usage: A want with an action in it — the everyday two-verb sentence.
sentences.mnemonic: veux + bare verb + the noun's own article. Three parts, none of them optional.

sentences.display: Je ne veux pas de café
sentences.literal: I not want not of coffee

words.note: The front half of the negation. It goes straight in front of the verb and is never enough alone — pas has to follow: je ne veux pas. Before a vowel it shortens to n' and welds on, hence L1-M9's n'ai.
The back half. It stands immediately after the verb, and it is what an ear actually hears — speech often drops the ne and never drops the pas. Writing keeps both.

sentences.trap: English negates with one word in front of the verb and an auxiliary to carry it — "do not want". French has no auxiliary and two words, one on each side of the verb. Reaching for a French "do" is reaching for something that does not exist.
sentences.sound: ne is a light duh sound, easily lost — and in speech it very often is. pas is pa, with the final -s silent, and it is the half that carries the meaning to the ear.

variations.display: Je ne veux pas de thé
variations.changed: swap the noun — the wrap and the bare de are the frame

variations.display: Vous ne voulez pas de café ?
variations.changed: voulez inside the same wrap, asked with a rising voice
take the wrap away and the partitive comes straight back: de → du

mistake.display: Je ne veux pas du café
mistake.why: Behind ne … pas every article collapses to a bare de: de café. du would be saying "some" inside a sentence that has just denied there is any.

sentences.usage: Refusing, in any register — and this is the polite refusal too.
sentences.mnemonic: ne … pas is a pair of brackets, and the verb sits inside them.

words.note: a, in front of a feminine noun — and, like un, also the number one. une voiture is "a car" and "one car" at once. Unlike un it is not nasal: the n is fully sounded.
car — feminine, so une voiture and la voiture.

sentences.trap: un and une look like a spelling difference and are not: un is nasal and une is not, so they are two clearly different sounds, and choosing wrongly is audible.
sentences.sound: une is ün — the French u with the n fully pronounced after it. voiture is vwa-TÜR, the same tight u again, with the r in the throat.

variations.changed: swap the feminine noun — une is the frame
voulez and a rising voice

variations.display: Je ne veux pas de voiture
variations.changed: une collapses to a bare de behind the negation, as every article does

mistake.why: voiture is feminine: une voiture. un beside it is the gender going unnoticed, and it is audible as well as visible.

sentences.mnemonic: un hums through the nose; une says its n out loud.

words.note: milk — masculine, so le lait and du lait. The final -t is silent, which makes it sound like the -ais of anglais.

sentences.trap: English needs "do" to make this a question. French adds nothing at all: the statement Vous voulez du lait becomes the question by the voice alone, plus the mark on the page.
sentences.sound: leh, one syllable, with the final -t silent. voulez is voo-LAY, the -ez ending sounding exactly like the -er of manger.

variations.changed: swap the mass noun — the offer is the frame
voulez → veux: the answer, in the first person, with no question mark

variations.display: Vous ne voulez pas de lait ?
variations.changed: the negation wraps voulez, and du collapses to de behind it

mistake.display: Est-ce que vous voulez du lait
mistake.why: Two things at once: this course asks with a rising voice and nothing else, and a question always carries its mark. Vous voulez du lait ?

sentences.usage: Offering something across a counter or a table.
sentences.mnemonic: -ez and -er sound the same: voulez, manger — both just ay.

words.note: to work — another bare -er form, following veux with nothing in between. The ill in the middle is a y sound, never an l: tra-va-YAY.

sentences.trap: The brackets close around the FIRST verb only. English would put the "not" next to "work"; French leaves travailler outside ne … pas altogether.
sentences.sound: tra-va-YAY. The r is in the throat, the ill is a y as in "yes", and the -er ending is the same clean ay as manger's.

variations.changed: swap the infinitive — it stays outside the brackets either way
voulez inside the wrap, asked with a rising voice
the brackets come away and nothing else changes

mistake.why: The negation wraps the verb that carries the person, and here that is veux: Je ne veux pas travailler.

sentences.usage: Refusing an activity rather than a thing.
sentences.mnemonic: The brackets go round the verb that changed for you, never round the bare one.
